To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the achievable rate of the causal filtering approach can be very close to that of the noncausal filtering approach, especially when the Doppler spread of the channel is small and/or when the number of training symbols is large, and that aliasing in the Doppler spectrum can significantly degrade the achievable rate of causal Wiener filters.

pilot-symbol-assisted transmission with a causal Wiener channel estimator is a viable alternative to noncausal filtering, and the energy-per-bit requirements for the two approaches are very similar for practical channel conditions.

pilot-assisted transmission with noncausal Wiener filtering achieves the same performance as pilot-assisted transmission without channel estimation and that pilot-assisted data transmission with causal Wiener filtering is a good approximation of pilot-assisted data transmissions with noncausal filtering.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the performance of noncausal Wiener filters, and the performance degradation incurred by using a noncausal Wierner filter instead of the optimal noncausal Wiemer filter.
the design of pilot-assisted communication schemes with noncausal Wiener filters, and the performance comparison with the more common causal filters.
the design and performance analysis of a pilot-assisted communication system that employs either a causal or noncausal Wiener filter to mitigate intersymbol interference.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the noncausal and the causal filters are comparable in terms of the achievable rates, but that the noncaausal filter is superior in terms of the energy-per-bit requirements.
, for practical ranges of the Doppler spectrum bandwidth, the performance of a causal filter is close to that of a noncausal one.

for a wide range of parameters of interest, the achievable rate and energy-per-bit performance of causal and non-causal filtering approaches are comparable, with the noncausal approach being superior.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the performance loss incurred in the use of the causal Wiener filter instead of the noncausal Wiener filter is very small.
pilot-assisted communication systems employing causal Wiener filters can achieve performance that is very close to that of systems with noncausal Wiener filters.
the performance loss incurred due to the use of a causal filter is small, but the energy-per-bit performance of the causal filter is better.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in the case of fast fading, the performance loss of a causal filter is not significant.
for practical ranges of Doppler frequencies, the performance loss due to using causal filters as opposed to noncausal filters is negligible.
for the particular range of Doppler spreads that we considered, the performance loss due to causal filtering is small.
